     Scales as <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d^{3})" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d3)\mathcal{O}(d^{3}) with the number of residual streams <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd, both in FLOP complexity and parameter count, surpassing the super-exponential scaling of mHC-lite and KromHC’s component factors.

|  | <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{J}_{d}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{J}_{d}=\mathbf{J}_{d}," class="ltx_Math" display="block" id="S2.Ex1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐌𝐉</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐉</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{J}_{d}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{J}_{d}=\mathbf{J}_{d},</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐌⊤​𝐉d=𝐌𝐉d=𝐉d,\mathbf{M}^{\top}\mathbf{J}_{d}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{J}_{d}=\mathbf{J}_{d}, |  |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |

mHC-lite ([Yang and Gao, 2026](#bib.bib3 "")) attempts to circumvent the approximation gap and customized kernel by making use of the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem to define the learned connections as a convex combination of the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d!" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d!</annotation></semantics></math> --> d!d! permutation matrices (where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd is the number of residual streams), at an <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d​C⋅d!)\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!) cost. This method works well for small <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd, however, this is not tenable in the limit of scaling <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d>8" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>></mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d>8</annotation></semantics></math> --> d>8d>8. KromHC ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib6 "")) sacrifices expressivity and complete coverage of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} by using tensor products to train residual connections on a much smaller set of exactly double-stochastic matrices with the added benefit of costing only <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d2​C)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C).

mHC-lite ([Yang and Gao, 2026](#bib.bib3 "")) attempts to circumvent the approximation gap and customized kernel by making use of the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem to define the learned connections as a convex combination of the <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d!" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d!</annotation></semantics></math> --> d!d! permutation matrices (where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd is the number of residual streams), at an <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d​C⋅d!)\mathcal{O}(dC\cdot d!) cost. This method works well for small <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> --> dd, however, this is not tenable in the limit of scaling <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d>8" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>></mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d>8</annotation></semantics></math> --> d>8d>8. KromHC ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib6 "")) sacrifices expressivity and complete coverage of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} by using tensor products to train residual connections on a much smaller set of exactly double-stochastic matrices with the added benefit of costing only <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C)</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝒪⁡(d2​C)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}C).

|  | <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{x}_{l+1}=\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{res}}\,\mathbf{x}_{l}+(\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{post}})^{\top}\,\mathcal{F}\!\left(\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{pre}}\,\mathbf{x}_{l},\,\mathbf{W}_{l}\right)," class="ltx_Math" display="block" id="S3.E1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mi>l</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mi>l</mi><mtext>post</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mpadded style="width:0.648em;" width="0.648em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mpadded><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mi>l</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{l+1}=\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{res}}\,\mathbf{x}_{l}+(\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{post}})^{\top}\,\mathcal{F}\!\left(\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{pre}}\,\mathbf{x}_{l},\,\mathbf{W}_{l}\right),</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐱l+1=ℋlres​𝐱l+(ℋlpost)⊤​ℱ​(ℋlpre​𝐱l,𝐖l),\mathbf{x}_{l+1}=\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{res}}\\,\mathbf{x}_{l}+(\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{post}})^{\top}\\,\mathcal{F}\\!\left(\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{pre}}\\,\mathbf{x}_{l},\\,\mathbf{W}_{l}\right), |  | (1) |

where the function skew maps vectors of size <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\frac{ds(ds-1)}{2}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{ds(ds-1)}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> --> d​s​(d​s−1)2\frac{ds(ds-1)}{2} to a <!-- MathML: <math alttext="ds\times ds" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds\times ds</annotation></semantics></math> --> d​s×d​sds\times ds skew-symmetric matrix <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\left(\mathbf{A}_{l}^{\top}=-\mathbf{A}_{l}\right)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(\mathbf{A}_{l}^{\top}=-\mathbf{A}_{l}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> --> (𝐀l⊤=−𝐀l)\left(\mathbf{A}_{l}^{\top}=-\mathbf{A}_{l}\right). Equation [8](#S3.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 3.3 Learning the 𝑠-Orthostochastic Manifold ‣ 3 go-mHC: Generalized Orthostochastic Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices") makes use of the Cayley transform to map <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{A}_{l}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐀l\mathbf{A}_{l} to the space of special orthogonal matrices <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\left(\mathbf{Q}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{l}=\mathbf{I}\right)" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐐</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(\mathbf{Q}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{l}=\mathbf{I}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> --> (𝐐l⊤​𝐐l=𝐈)\left(\mathbf{Q}_{l}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}_{l}=\mathbf{I}\right). We can then use <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\Phi_{d,s}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{d,s}</annotation></semantics></math> --> Φd,s\Phi_{d,s} from equation [6](#S3.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 3.2 Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices ‣ 3 go-mHC: Generalized Orthostochastic Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices") to map <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathbf{Q}_{l}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐐l\mathbf{Q}_{l} to an exactly doubly stochastic matrix <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{res}}\in\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mi>l</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{res}}\in\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> ℋlres∈𝖡d\mathcal{H}_{l}^{\text{res}}\in\mathsf{B}_{d} in equation [9](#S3.E9 "Equation 9 ‣ 3.3 Learning the 𝑠-Orthostochastic Manifold ‣ 3 go-mHC: Generalized Orthostochastic Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections ‣ go-mHC: Direct Parameterization of Manifold-ConstrainedHyper-Connections via Generalized Orthostochastic Matrices").

|  | <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\displaystyle\text{AGM}^{\text{fwd}}(\mathcal{H}_{l\to L}^{\text{res}})=\max_{i}\sum_{j}|(\mathcal{H}_{l\to L}^{\text{res}})_{ij}|," class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S3.E10.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mtext>AGM</mtext><mtext>fwd</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mtext>res</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mmultiscripts><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><mprescripts /><mi>i</mi><mrow /></mmultiscripts></mstyle><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mtext>res</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{AGM}^{\text{fwd}}(\mathcal{H}_{l\to L}^{\text{res}})=\max_{i}\sum_{j}|(\mathcal{H}_{l\to L}^{\text{res}})_{ij}|,</annotation></semantics></math> --> AGMfwd​(ℋl→Lres)=max⁡∑ji⁡|(ℋl→Lres)i​j|,\displaystyle\text{AGM}^{\text{fwd}}(\mathcal{H}_{l\to L}^{\text{res}})=\max_{i}\sum_{j}|(\mathcal{H}_{l\to L}^{\text{res}})_{ij}|, |  | (10) |

The eigenvalue distribution of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="d\times d" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times d</annotation></semantics></math> --> d×dd\times d <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> --> ss-orthostochastic matrices is fundamentally constrained by their membership in the Birkhoff polytope <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} and residence within the Karpelevič region. While <!-- MathML: <math alttext="1" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m4" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> --> 11-orthostochastic matrices exhibit a restricted, hypo-cycloidal boundary, increasing the parameter <!-- MathML: <math alttext="s" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m5" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> --> ss provides a progressively denser approximation of the full <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\mathsf{B}_{d}" class="ltx_Math" display="inline" id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m6" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝖡</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathsf{B}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝖡d\mathsf{B}_{d} ([Nechita et al., 2023](#bib.bib4 "")).
